The public single-cell RNA sequencing datasets used in this study can be found in Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) with the accession number GSE127465 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE127465), GSE123904 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE123904), GSE131907 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE131907) and GSE117529 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE117529), in BioStudies with accession number E-MTAB-13526 (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biostudies/arrayexpress/studies/E-MTAB-13526), from Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/8227624) or in the LungCancer website (https://lungcancer.chenlulab.com/#/download). The public ST data of NSCLC can be found in BioStudies with accession number E-MTAB-13530 (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biostudies/arrayexpress/studies/E-MTAB-13530). The public ST data of mLNs in breast cancer can be found in GEO with accession number GSE190811 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE190811). The ST data of nLN was from 10X Genomics website (https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets/human-lymph-node-1-standard-1-1-0). Bulk RNA-seq data was from the cancer genome atlas (TCGA) and GEO (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE30219; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE68465). Source Data are provided with this paper.

Code availability
Code is available from github (https://github.com/diChen310/mLN_NSCLC/, DOI: http://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18690124) 139.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This study by Chen et al. aims to understand lymph node metastasis in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) by integrating single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) data from matched primary tumors and metastatic lymph nodes (mLNs). Main findings include the identification of two distinct mechanisms underlying lymph node metastasis and immune evasion: one driven by cancer stemness and ferroptosis resistance, and the other mediated by malignant-cell-derived immunoglobulins at the tumor periphery. The study also reveals a key role of fibroblasts in forming a physical barrier that separates immune cells from tumor epithelial cells, while also contributing to cell transitions. Furthermore, the authors find that tumor microenvironment (TME) in both mLNs and metastatic-primary tumors (mLN⁺ PTs) are enriched with immunosuppressive cell types, including SPP1⁺IFI30⁺ macrophages, CXCL13⁺ exhausted T cells, and hyperactivated B cells. The authors use independent single-cell datasets, TCGA-LUAD bulk RNA-seq data, and functional experiments to validate the findings. This work not only provides a comprehensive view of the cellular and molecular landscape of lymph node metastasis but also offers valuable datasets to study cancer biology, immunology, and therapeutic strategy for NSCLC and potentially other tumors. The manuscript is written clearly overall. However, we have several specific comments that the authors should address to enhance the clarity of interpretation and the strength of the conclusions.
Major concerns:
1. For “stemness” analysis, the authors use CytoTRACE to infer stemness scores, where a higher score reflects greater stemness or lower differentiation. However, given that Monocle3 was used for pre-processing the data and generating trajectories. If their results are consistent, they seem redundant: why not just using Monocle3 to infer pseudotime for inferring stemness? If the results are different, how to interpret the discrepancies? In other words, how robust are the CytoTRACE-derived stemness scores? Has any form of validation (e.g., correlation with known stemness markers other than CD44 and ENO1) been conducted?
2. Cell-cell interaction analysis results need more clarification and/or validation. For example, in the cell neighborhood analysis, the number of cell-cell neighbors (CCNs) are counted based on the dominant cell type of two spots. How are dominant cell types within each spot defined? For example, if a spot contains a 50/50 mix of epithelial and myeloid cells, how is this ambiguity resolved?
3. The authors identified interactions between CXCL14⁺ T cells and B cells, and between CAFs and LAMP3⁺ dendritic cells based on CellChat results. Given the availability of spatial transcriptomic data, is there any quantitative assessment of spatial proximity to support these inferred interactions? Similarly, on page 21, the interaction between SPP1⁺ macrophages and both malignant cells and exhausted T cells is noted. Can these interactions be spatially validated?
4. Spatial transcriptomics data analysis requires clearer and more rigorous presentation. For example, on page 18, the authors refer to fibroblasts being “in close proximity” to epithelial cells. How is this spatial proximity quantitatively defined? Likewise, on page 21, how are spots categorized as “near” or “far” from myeloid cells? What is the spatial threshold or metric used to make this classification?
5. Biological relevance of identified marker genes needs better explanation and discussion. For example, the analysis of fibroblasts highlights CST1⁺ fibroblasts as being specific to mLNs and mLN⁺ PTs. However, the functional relevance of CST1 is not discussed. Providing biological context or prior evidence for its significance would strengthen the rationale for focusing on this subpopulation. Similar clarification is warranted for ALDOA⁺, ARHGAP15⁺, and CXCL13⁺ T cells. Why were these genes selected for emphasis, and what is their biological or clinical importance?
Minor concerns:
6. On page 24, the term “other exhausted T cells” is used, and these cells appear to be specific to mLNs. Given their apparent specificity, is there anything interesting about them?
7. Figure 1E: Spots with higher feature values are displayed with lighter colors, which is visually counterintuitive.
8. Figure 2D: It is unclear whether the color gradient reflects CytoTRACE scores or relative gene expression. Additionally, the term "relative expression" is ambiguous. Does it refer to normalized expressions or something else? The legends should be clarified, since it currently refers to "correlated gene expression."
9. Figure 4H: It would be helpful to clarify what is being correlated. Is it the abundance of the fibroblast subpopulation versus the abundance of other cell types within each mLN⁺ sample, or something else?
10. Figure 4G: The y-axis label should be "CCN" (cell-cell neighbors), not "CNN."
11. Figure 5D: The x-axis label should be consistently presented as "mLN vs nLN" instead of "mln".

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, Chen et al. present a comprehensive investigation into the mechanisms of lymph node (LN) metastasis in NSCLC using a multimodal omics approach, including single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), spatial transcriptomics (ST), and bulk RNA sequencing. The study characterizes the tumor microenvironment (TME) of metastatic LNs (mLNs) and matched primary tumors (mLN+ PTs), providing novel insights into cancer stemness, immune evasion, and spatial organization driving metastasis. The findings offer significant translational potential for understanding NSCLC progression and developing novel therapies.
The work provides valuable contributions to our understanding of LN metastasis by providing a comprehensive multimodal omics resource for dissecting TME heterogeneity. This study holds potential implications for immunotherapy. Most notably, the identification of FTH1-driven ferroptosis resistance as a key driver of cancer stemness and metastasis builds upon emerging ferroptosis research while offering novel insights through its specific focus on LN metastasis and innovative integration with spatial transcriptomics data. The discovery of immunoglobulin expression by malignant cells represents another intriguing finding with potential implications for immune evasion. Furthermore, the detailed characterization of the immunosuppressive TME, particularly the mechanisms of immune exclusion, significantly advances the field and highlights promising therapeutic targets such as FTH1 and CXCL13. Overall, the study is comprehensive and well-structured by multimodal data, validation across independent datasets, as well as in vitro and in vivo experiments.
Concerns and suggestions for improvement:
- The potential link between ferroptosis/FTH1 and LN metastasis is compelling but remains speculative, if feasible, experimental validation would strengthen the claim.
-The proposed functions of tumor-derived immunoglobulins also remain speculative, if feasible, functional assays could clarify their impact.
- Given histological distinctions in NSCLC, comparing LUAD and LUSC could reveal subtype-specific metastatic mechanisms.
-Please define key abbreviations (e.g., mLN, mLN+ PT, LN+N) in figure legends when first introduced.
-Please clarify criteria for defining tumor core vs. periphery in ST data
-Please Justify thresholds for gene expression cutoffs (eg. how "immunoglobulin-high" malignant cells were classified)
-If feasible, may consider analyzing whether SPP1+IFI30+ macrophages or CXCL13+ T cells correlate with immunotherapy resistance in clinical cohorts.
-In the discussion section, please consider further addressing clinical translation and therapeutic implications, as well as comparing NSCLC metastasis to other solid tumors.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The manuscript profiles matched metastatic lymph nodes and primary tumors from 19 NSCLC patients using scRNA-seq (848,337 cells) and Visium ST (4 matched pairs), integrating public datasets to dissect cellular and spatial programs underlying LN metastasis. The authors report high stemness in mLN/mLN+ PT epithelial cells, discovery of immunoglobulin-high malignant cells expressing PD-L1, fibroblast-driven immune exclusion at tumor edges, enrichment of SPP1+IFI30+ macrophages and CXCL13+ exhausted T cells in LS-like regions, and implicate ferroptosis/FTH1 in metastasis with functional validation. The work is timely and offers an integrative cellular–spatial view of LN metastasis. The dataset is valuable, but several analytical choices, and reporting gaps limit reproducibility and interpretability.
Major concerns:
-Only 4 mLN/mLN+ PT pairs underwent ST; no normal LN or additional metastatic sites were profiled spatially, limiting generalizability and statistical power for spatial claims in the paper.
-LS-like spots are defined by co-expression of MS4A1, TRBC2, CXCL13, CCL19, CCL21 without any orthogonal validation (imaging, IHC). The methodology for “two-step neighbors” is computationally defined and may overestimate aggregation. The authors should provide histologic confirmation (such as CD20, CD3, BCL6 staining) or cite prior validation of this marker-based LS/TLS call.
-Batch correction is explicitly skipped for malignant cells “to retain patient specificity,” which risks inflating inter-patient differences in downstream clustering and DE. The authors should show that their key findings (Ig-high clusters, stemness gradients) persist under an alternative integration (eg Harmony, etc) using additional sensitivity analysis.
-The methodology for spatial analysis need to be clarified. For example, the edge/core classification uses median distance thresholds, which could be sample-size dependent. The authors need to provide justification.
-Also, LS like spot identification and two-step neighbor definition are described, but criteria for LS like designation are not detailed (which gene sets? morphology?)
-Numerous Wilcoxon tests and GSEA are reported, FDR control is stated but not consistently shown for all comparisons. Clarify all thresholds used.
Minor points:
-Some typos need to be corrected: “matirx” ; “contral” ; “princeple” ; “probalility” ; “up-regualted” . Please run a thorough copy edit.
-There are issues with acronyms, please define all at first use (e.g., “mCAF”, “tCAF”, “SC7”, “LS-like”).
-Provide exact gene lists for CSC, SPP1⁺IFI30⁺ MP, and CXCL13⁺ T signatures used in validations for reproducibility.

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author): bioinformatic analysis of omics data including ST

The authors use independent single-cell datasets, TCGA-LUAD bulk RNA-seq data, and functional experiments to validate the findings. This work not only provides a comprehensive view of the cellular and molecular landscape of lymph node metastasis but also offers valuable datasets to study cancer biology, immunology, and therapeutic strategy for NSCLC and potentially other tumors. Re: Thanks a lot for the affirmation of our work and the valuable suggestions. We have revised the manuscript according to the comments and suggestions.
Major concerns:
1. For “stemness” analysis, the authors use CytoTRACE to infer stemness scores, where a higher score reflects greater stemness or lower differentiation. However, given that Monocle3 was used for pre-processing the data and generating trajectories. If their results are consistent, they seem redundant: why not just using Monocle3 to infer pseudotime for inferring stemness? If the results are different, how to interpret the discrepancies? In other words, how robust are the CytoTRACE-derived stemness scores? Has any form of validation (e.g., correlation with known stemness markers other than CD44 and ENO1) been conducted?
RE: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful question regarding the relationship between CytoTRACE-derived stemness scores and Monocle3 pseudotime. Below, we clarify our rationale and present evidence supporting the robustness of our approach:
While Monocle3 is powerful for trajectory inference, its pseudotime calculation requires user-specified root nodes (as noted in the Monocle3 tutorial, https://cole-trapnell-lab.github.io/monocle3/docs/trajectories/#learn-graph). This introduces subjectivity, as the choice of root nodes (often based on prior knowledge or assumptions) directly influences pseudotime values. In contrast, CytoTRACE objectively infers stemness solely from gene expression signatures, without requiring user input on root nodes.
To address the reviewer’s concern, we explicitly tested the correlation between CytoTRACE scores and Monocle3 pseudotime, where the cells with high CytoTRACE scores were selected as the root nodes. The results were displayed as below:
Figure R1_1. Umap visualization of the CytoTRACE and Pseudotime values of the epithelial cells in LUAD and LUSC respectively.
We calculated the correlations between CytoTRACE scores and the pseudotime values:
For LUAD, Spearman’s ρ = -0.40 (p < 2.2e-16).
For LUSC, Spearman’s ρ = -0.38 (p < 2.2e-16).
The significant negative correlations confirm that cells with high CytoTRACE scores (greater stemness) align with early pseudotime states (root nodes), as expected biologically.
Though consistent, CytoTRACE was chosen as the primary metric of cell stemness because the following reasons:
1) CytoTRACE does not require manually selected root nodes
2) CytoTRACE specializes in stemness prediction (unlike Monocle3’s broader trajectory focus),
3) Monocle3 here was mainly applied for the pre-processing, reduction and clustering analysis of the scRNA-seq data, since a benchmark study for scRNA-seq analysis tools demonstrated that Monocle3 also displayed good performance for the general clustering analysis of the scRNA-seq data [1].
4) We further validated CytoTRACE scores by confirming their agreement with known stemness markers (e.g., CD44, EpCAM, CD166), see Figure 2E and Page 8-9, Line 155-157, as below:
CD44, EpCAM and CD166 (gene names CD44, EPCAM and ALCAM) are widely recognized markers of CSCs in NSCLC [2, 3]. Here, epithelial cells exhibiting high CytoTRACE scores also showed a significant higher expression of CD44, EPCAM and ALCAM (Figure 2E).
Figure 2E. Box plot showing the differential expressions of stemness marker genes CD44, EPCAM and ALCAM in epithelial cells with high or low CytoTRACE scores in LUAD and LUSC respectively. High and low is separated by the median value of CytoTRACE scores. ****p < 0.0001 by Wilcox-test, unpaired, two-sided.
References:
1. Yu, L., et al., Benchmarking clustering algorithms on estimating the number of cell types from single-cell RNA-sequencing data. Genome Biol, 2022. 23(1): p. 49.
2. Zakaria, N., et al., Human non-small cell lung cancer expresses putative cancer stem cell markers and exhibits the transcriptomic profile of multipotent cells. BMC Cancer, 2015. 15: p. 84.
3. Zhang, W.C., et al., Glycine decarboxylase activity drives non-small cell lung cancer tumor-initiating cells and tumorigenesis. Cell, 2012. 148(1-2): p. 259-72.
2. Cell-cell interaction analysis results need more clarification and/or validation. For example, in the cell neighborhood analysis, the number of cell-cell neighbors (CCNs) are counted based on the dominant cell type of two spots. How are dominant cell types within each spot defined? For example, if a spot contains a 50/50 mix of epithelial and myeloid cells, how is this ambiguity resolved?
RE: We appreciate the reviewer's insightful question regarding the definition of dominant cell in spatial spots. Below we provide a detailed clarification of our methodology and the relevant results.
The definition of dominant cell types for the spots were based on the spatial clustering results. Here, the dominant cell types of each spatial cluster was annotated based on whether the cluster showed significantly higher expressions of classical marker genes of the major cell types. A spatial cluster could be assigned more than one cell type (e.g., Plasma+Myeloid) if markers from multiple cell types met the thresholds, reflecting the spatial co-localization of different cell types. The spatial annotation results are shown in Figure 1D and S1D.
We have clarify the relevant definition and analysis methods in the Methods sections, in Page 51, Line 1043-1052 , as below:
Spatial annotation of SD data
Over expressed marker genes of each spatial cluster were identified using FindAllMarkers function in Seurat, with the following thresholds: avg_log2FC> 0.1, P.adj<0.01, pct.1 > 0.3, and ranked top-8 based on log2FC. The "near" versus "far" categorization of myeloid spots relative to epithelial spots was determined as:

Definition of epithelial-near/far based on the distances with epithelial spots

According to the spatial coordinates of Visium, the distance between two adjacent spots in the same line equals 2, and between two adjacent spots from two different lines equals 1.414, and two-step neighbors (i.e., neighbors’ neighbors) were with min-distance <= 4. Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author): lung cancer metastasis and immune evasion
In this manuscript, Chen et al. present a comprehensive investigation into the mechanisms of lymph node (LN) metastasis in NSCLC using a multimodal omics approach, including single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), spatial transcriptomics (ST), and bulk RNA sequencing. The study characterizes the tumor microenvironment (TME) of metastatic LNs (mLNs) and matched primary tumors (mLN+ PTs), providing novel insights into cancer stemness, immune evasion, and spatial organization driving metastasis. The findings offer significant translational potential for understanding NSCLC progression and developing novel therapies.
The work provides valuable contributions to our understanding of LN metastasis by providing a comprehensive multimodal omics resource for dissecting TME heterogeneity. This study holds potential implications for immunotherapy. Most notably, the identification of FTH1-driven ferroptosis resistance as a key driver of cancer stemness and metastasis builds upon emerging ferroptosis research while offering novel insights through its specific focus on LN metastasis and innovative integration with spatial transcriptomics data. The discovery of immunoglobulin expression by malignant cells represents another intriguing finding with potential implications for immune evasion. Furthermore, the detailed characterization of the immunosuppressive TME, particularly the mechanisms of immune exclusion, significantly advances the field and highlights promising therapeutic targets such as FTH1 and CXCL13. Overall, the study is comprehensive and well-structured by multimodal data, validation across independent datasets, as well as in vitro and in vivo experiments.

RE: We have revised the method section in Line ** ,as below:
Determination of tumor core and peripheral partitions for epithelial spots
Based on the assumption that non-epithelial spots primarily represent non-tumor components of the microenvironment, for each epithelial spot on every ST slice, we calculated the minimum Euclidean distance between this spot and all the other non-epithelial cells using the spots’ coordinates. Here, a small distance indicates closer proximity to non-tumor regions and, by extension, far from the tumor core. Then, epithelial spots with minimum distances below the median value of all epithelial spots on the same ST slice were classified as belonging to the tumor periphery; the remaining epithelial spots were assigned to the tumor core region.

-LS-like spots are defined by co-expression of MS4A1, TRBC2, CXCL13, CCL19, CCL21 without any orthogonal validation (imaging, IHC). The methodology for “two-step neighbors” is computationally defined and may overestimate aggregation. The authors should provide histologic confirmation (such as CD20, CD3, BCL6 staining) or cite prior validation of this marker-based LS/TLS call.
RE: We thank the reviewer for raising these important points regarding the definition and validation of LS-like structures. Below we provide a detailed response addressing both the marker selection and histological correlation.
Biological basis for LS/TLS marker selection:
MS4A1 (CD20) is a cell surface protein primarily found on B cells and is a common marker used to identify B cell follicles within TLS [1]. TRBC2 encodes a component of the T cell receptor, and its expression is indicative of T cell presence within the TLS[2]. The chemokines CXCL13, CCL19, and CCL21 are vital for recruiting immune cells, particularly B cells and T cells, into the tumor microenvironment to form TLS. CXCL13 is produced by T cells and follicular dendritic cells within TLS, attracting CXCR5+ B and T cells [2]. CCL19 and CCL21, produced by fibroblasts and other cell types, also contribute to cell recruitment [3]. Consequently, this combination of the markers (MS4A1, TRBC2, CXCL13, CCL19, CCL21) are supported by the literature for identifying TLS and lymphoid aggregates. We have cited these references to validate this marker-based LS/TLS annotations.
References:
1. Fridman, W.H., et al., Tertiary lymphoid structures and B cells: An intratumoral immunity cycle. Immunity, 2023. 56(10): p. 2254-2269.
2. Sautes-Fridman, C., et al., Tertiary lymphoid structures in the era of cancer immunotherapy. Nature Reviews Cancer, 2019. 19(6): p. 307-325.
3. Zhang, Y., et al., CCL19-producing fibroblasts promote tertiary lymphoid structure formation enhancing anti-tumor IgG response in colorectal cancer liver metastasis. Cancer Cell, 2024. 42(8): p. 1370-1385.e9.
Methodological clarification:
The LS-like spots identified in our analysis encompass both residual lymphoid structures and tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS). The LS-like spots were annotated according to the spatial clustering results, rather than “two-step neighbors” method, we have revised the method part to more explicitly state about spatial annotation method, in Page 51, Line 1043-1051, as below:
Spatial annotation of ST data
Over expressed marker genes of each spatial cluster were identified using FindAllMarkers function in Seurat, with the following thresholds: avg_log2FC> 0.1, P.adj<0.01, pct.1 > 0.3, and ranked top-8 based on log2FC. The spatial clusters were annotated based on whether the cluster marker genes included the classical marker genes of the major cell types including epithelial (SCGB3A1, KRT5, SFTPB, SFTPA1,S100A2, AKR1C1, CES1 ), fibroblast (COL1A1, COL1A2, ACTA2, FN1), myeloid (LYZ, C1QB, TYROBP), plasma (IGHG1, IGHG3, MZB1, JCHAIN) and LS-like structures (CXCL13, CCL19, CCL21, MS4A1 and TRBC2) [20-23]. One spatial cluster can be assigned with more than one cell type owing to the co-localization of different cell types spatially. Meanwhile, spatial clusters showing high expressions of mitochondria genes were annotated as MT-high.
The description about the LS-like spots were in Page 4, Line 113-118, as below:
Notably, two of the spatial clusters (SC3 and SC4) showed simultaneous high expressions of MS4A1, TRBC2 (Figures 1D and S1D), indicating the aggregation of T and B cells [20]. The two clusters also showed high expressions of CXCL13, CCL19 and CCL21 (Figures 1D and S1D), all of which contribute to the formation of secondary and tertiary LS (TLS) [36-38]. These two clusters were annotated as LS-like spots, representing the residual LSs in the mLNs, and potential TLSs in the mLN+ PTs or mLN- PTs.
Histopathological validation:
With guidance from clinical pathologists, we marked LS-like regions in the spatial transcriptomics data based on corresponding H&E-stained tissue sections.
Furthermore, we have included zoomed-in views of two representative regions (new Figures 1D and 1E) to demonstrate strong concordance between the computationally annotated spatial clusters and histopathological assessment.
Figure 1. Overview of the TME landscape of LN metastatic NSCLC
(D) Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images and ST based spot-annotation results of the paired mLN+ PTs and mLNs from four patients. Each ST spot is colored according to the clustering and annotation results.
(E) Enlarged regions of interest (ROIs) containing LS-like spots, including TLS in mLN+ PT and residual LS in mLN. Corresponding ROIs are outlined in red boxes in panel (D).
-Batch correction is explicitly skipped for malignant cells “to retain patient specificity,” which risks inflating inter-patient differences in downstream clustering and DE. The authors should show that their key findings (Ig-high clusters, stemness gradients) persist under an alternative integration (eg Harmony, etc) using additional sensitivity analysis.
RE: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. In response, we have performed Harmony-based batch correction for the analysis of malignant cells to evaluate the robustness of our key findings. These results found that Ig-high clusters and CytoTRACE scores showed similar trends as identified by the previous analysis.
We have added these results in Figures S3F-S3I, as below:
Figure S3. Elevated expression of immunoglobulin genes in epithelial cells of mLNs and mLN+ PTs
(F) Umap plot showing the harmony-corrected clustering results of malignant cells. Harmony correction was applied on the PCA reductions to remove batch effects among different patients.
(G) Dot plot showing the mean expression of classical marker genes of AT2/basal and immunoglobulin genes across the harmon-corrected malignant cell clusters. Clusters exhibiting significantly elevated expressions of Ig-genes (IGHG1, IGHG4, IGHA1 or IGHG2; examined by likelihood ratio test, Benjamini Hochberg adjusted P < 0.01 and mean_expression > 10) are highlighted by red fonts and termed as Ig-high clusters, and the others as Ig-low clusters.
(H) Box plot of the CytoTRACE scores in the harmon-corrected Ig-high and Ig-low malignant cell clusters.
(I) Violin plot comparing the normalized expression of CD274 in the harmon-corrected Ig-high and Ig-low malignant cell clusters. The point in the middle marks the median value.
and we have added description in the results section, Page 12, Line 224-228, as below:
Meanwhile, we conducted parallel clustering analyses of malignant cells - one preserving patient-specific batch effects and one with batch effect correction, to ensure robust results (Methods). Both results showed that some of the clusters presented elevated expressions of immunoglobulin genes than the other clusters (Figures 3D-3F and S3E-S3G). Notably, the malignant cells expressing high levels of immunoglobulin genes displayed significantly lower CytoTRACE scores than those with low immunoglobulin expressions (Figures 3G and S3H).
-The methodology for spatial analysis need to be clarified. For example, the edge/core classification uses median distance thresholds, which could be sample-size dependent. The authors need to provide justification.
RE: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment regarding the spatial partitioning method. We have revised the Methods section to provide a more detailed description of the tumor core/periphery partition method, Page 52, Line 1068-1075 as follows:
Determination of tumor core and peripheral partitions for epithelial spots
Based on the assumption that non-epithelial spots primarily represent non-tumor components of the microenvironment, for each epithelial spot on every ST slice, we calculated the minimum Euclidean distance between this spot and all the other non-epithelial cells using the spots’ coordinates. Here, a small distance indicates closer proximity to non-tumor regions and, by extension, far from the tumor core. Then, epithelial spots with minimum distances below the median value of all epithelial spots on the same ST slice were classified as belonging to the tumor periphery; the remaining epithelial spots were assigned to the tumor core region.
Here, the median distance was computed independently for each ST slice, ensuring that the partition is based on a sample-specific threshold, not influenced by sample-size.

This marker set is consistent with previously published definitions of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) and lymphoid aggregates [1-3].

Two-step neighbors of the LS-like spots were used to investigate the neighborhood surrounding LS-like regions, but not for definition of LS-like spots. we have revised the method part to more explicitly state about spatial annotation method, in Page 51, Line 1043-1051.
References:
1. Fridman, W.H., et al., Tertiary lymphoid structures and B cells: An intratumoral immunity cycle. Immunity, 2023. 56(10): p. 2254-2269.
2. Sautes-Fridman, C., et al., Tertiary lymphoid structures in the era of cancer immunotherapy. Nature Reviews Cancer, 2019. 19(6): p. 307-325.
3. Zhang, Y., et al., CCL19-producing fibroblasts promote tertiary lymphoid structure formation enhancing anti-tumor IgG response in colorectal cancer liver metastasis. Cancer Cell, 2024. 42(8): p. 1370-1385.e9.
-Numerous Wilcoxon tests and GSEA are reported, FDR control is stated but not consistently shown for all comparisons. Clarify all thresholds used.
RE: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding multiple testing correction. We have carefully reviewed and clarified all statistical thresholds applied throughout our study, as detailed below:
Validation-oriented single gene tests (e.g., marker gene validation or hypothesis-driven comparisons of pre-specified genes) were assessed using uncorrected Wilcox-test, as is conventional for focused, confirmatory analyses.
Exploratory multi-gene comparisons (e.g., differential expression across cell types or conditions involving the whole gene list), p-values were subjected to Benjamini–Hochberg correction.
Gene Set/pathway enrichment analysis was performed in an exploratory manner, and all reported pathway enrichment results include Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted P-values.
All figure legends have been updated to unambiguously indicate the specific statistical thresholds and correction methods used in each analysis.
Minor points:
-Some typos need to be corrected: “matirx” ; “contral” ; “princeple” ; “probalility” ; “up-regualted” . Please run a thorough copy edit.
RE: We have revised them.
-There are issues with acronyms, please define all at first use (e.g., “mCAF”, “tCAF”, “SC7”, “LS-like”).
RE: We have checked acronyms and make sure we define all at first use.
-Provide exact gene lists for CSC, SPP1⁺IFI30⁺ MP, and CXCL13⁺ T signatures used in validations for reproducibility.
RE: The gene lists were provided in Table S2.
Here, according to the Editor and Reviewers’ important suggestions and comments, we have revised carefully and have made corrections which we hope to meet with approval. We attached the response letter and revised manuscript and the corrections are colored in red to make the revisions notable. The “Calibri” fonts cited the Editor and Reviewers’ comments, and the “Times new roman” and “Blue” fonts are our replies. The “Red” fonts are cited in the manuscript for helping the editor and reviewers easily read. If any question arises, please do not hesitate to let us know.

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Most concerns have been sufficiently addressed, and the revised manuscript has been substantially improved. However, there are several minor issues with the additional cell type co-localization analysis.
1. In Figure S7E, the spatial distribution of CXCL13⁺T cells and iCAF appears largely non-overlapping, with minimal spatial co-localization. This observation seems inconsistent with the main text claiming their co-localization within LS-like spots. Although cell-cell interactions do not necessarily require stringent co-localization, as exemplified by the proposed long-distance interaction between SPP1⁺macrophages and malignant epithelial cells in Figure S5H, the discrepancy between visual spatial pattern and the claim of colocalization requires clarification or quantitative spatial proximity measurement to substantiate the interpretation.
RE: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this comment and the opportunity to clarify. The reviewer is absolutely correct in their visual assessment of Figure S7E, the distribution of iCAFs is indeed broader and less perfectly overlapping with the dense cores of CXCL13+ T cells.
In our previous analysis, we calculated the co-localization scores across all spots, and compared the results in spot level, which did not account for sample-level variability. To address this, we have now performed a revised analysis at the sample level. Specifically, for each biological sample, we calculated the average co-localization scores separately for LS-like spots and all other spots within the sample.
The revised figure and figure legend are as below:
Figure S7F. Violin plots showing the sample-averaged co-localization scores between CXCL13+ T cells and their interacting cells, calculated specifically within LS-like spots or all other spots across mLN and mLN+PT samples. The co-localization score between CXCL13+ T cell and a partner cell type for one spot was calculated as the sum of the CARD-derived abundance scores of CXCL13+ T cell and the partner cell type. T-test, un-paired, one-sided.
The corresponding results have been revised as below (Page 25, Line 481-485):
CARD-based deconvolution analysis of the ST data also showed CXCL13+ T cells were significantly co-localized with key interacting cells, including LAMP3+ DCs, GC B cells, and activated B cells, within LS-like spots (Figures S7E and S7F). 2. In Figure S7F, the y-axis appears to be mislabeled. It should be “Sum score with CXCL13⁺T” instead of “CSCL”.
Re: We apologize for this error. We have revised this.
3. The method for calculating the summed abundance score requires clarification. Is it defined as the sum of the abundance scores of CXCL13⁺ T cells and the interacting cell type, or based on another formulation?
Re: We thank the reviewer for prompting us to clarify this. The method is defined as the sum of the abundance scores of CXCL13+ T cells and the interacting cell type. To make this clear, we have updated the figure legend for S7F, as below:
The co-localization score between CXCL13+ T cell and a partner cell type for one spot was calculated as the sum of the CARD-derived abundance scores of CXCL13+ T cell and the partner cell type.

Re: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree that a one-sided test is more appropriate. Accordingly, we have re-analyzed the data using a one-sided, unpaired T-test. This choice offers greater statistical power than a non-parametric test. For completeness, we also performed a one-sided Wilcox test, which yielded consistent significance conclusions. The results from the T-test are now reported in Figure S7F.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Cancer metastasis accounts for the majority of cancer-related deaths and lymph node metastasis is critical in cancer staging and prognosis. However, the mechanisms involved in lymph node metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain unclear. Here, we delineate the cellular and spatial landscape of metastatic lymph nodes and their matched primary tumors in NSCLC using multimodal omics. In results, tumor core and peripheral regions respectively exhibit high stemness and elevated expression of immunoglobulins. Increased expressions of CD274 (PD-L1) are observed in the immunoglobulin-high malignant cells and SPP1+IFI30+ macrophages. Notably, residual and tertiary lymphoid structures are identified. However, their anti-tumor immunity is compromised by CXCL13+ T cell exhaustion and immune exclusion. Furthermore, we identify the ferroptosis signaling, with its key factor FTH1 showing strong associations with cancer cell stemness and metastasis. This study elucidates the mechanisms of metastasis and immune evasion in lymph node metastatic NSCLC, providing insights for targeted therapies.

---

## Introduction

Lung cancer is the most common cause of cancer-related death around the world, and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most dominating histologic subtype 1. Approximately 80–90% of lung cancer-related deaths are caused by metastasis 2. Lymph nodes (LNs) play critical roles in the arrest and proliferation of metastatic cells, facilitate secondary dissemination to distant organs, and are integral to immune modulation in cancer 3, 4, 5. It has been validated that LN metastasis can predict poor prognostic outcomes in various types of cancer 6, 7, and is also a very common factor in NSCLC 1. Lymph node dissection is regarded as a standard surgery for NSCLC, contributing to accurate tumor staging and improved prognosis 8.

The potential molecular basis of LN metastasis is complicated and involves multiple processes and factors 3, 9, and current researches are mainly focused on lymph-angiogenesis 10, 11, malignant cell migration towards LNs 12, formation of premetastatic niche 13, immune evasion 14 and metabolic adaptation 15. Nonetheless, the mechanism underlying LN metastasis is still limited understood, more precise investigations are needed to obtain comprehensive insights into the LN and long distance metastasis.

Recent advances in single cell and spatial omics provide effective tools to explore the heterogeneous molecular functions and spatial organization of tumor microenvironment (TME) at a high resolution, promoting the understanding of cellular landscape and key mechanisms in cancer 16, 17, 18, 19, 20. A collection of single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies have been conducted on NSCLC 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29. These studies have presented the cellular and transcriptional landscape of cancer cells, immune cells and stromal cells in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and lung squamous-cell carcinoma (LUSC) 21, 27, early-stage LUAD harboring EGFR mutations 22, metastatic LUAD 23 and treatment relevant lung cancers 25, 30, 31. Differences between LUAD and LUSC have also been investigated 21, 28. Meanwhile, spatial transcriptomics (ST) studies have revealed some spatial features of NSCLC 20, 21, 24. Several scRNA-seq studies also explored the cellular features of metastatic lymph nodes (mLNs) in breast cancer 32 and head and neck cancer 33. However, the cellular and spatial characteristics of mLNs in NSCLC remain unclear, with only limited study about the cellular characteristics of mLNs in LUAD 23. There is currently a lack of systematic collection and integrative analysis of patient-matched mLNs and primary tumor tissues (mLN+ PTs) of NSCLC, which impedes the ability to trace malignant cells and TME between mLNs and their corresponding primary tumors, thereby limiting the depth and scope of such analyses.

Here, we aim to investigate the TME characteristics in both mLNs and primary tumor tissues that may promote metastasis to LNs, using multimodal omics including scRNA-seq, ST and bulk RNA-seq. The cellular features of mLNs are described by integrative and comparative analysis of the scRNA-seq data of patient-matched mLN, mLN+ PT and mLN-positive adjacent normal lung (mLN+ N) samples, as well as the other contrastive samples including normal LN (nLN), mLN negative primary lung tumor (mLN- PT) and adjacent normal lung (mLN- N) samples. Meanwhile, the spatially specific characteristics, particularly the lymphoid structure like (LS-like) and immune exclusion spatial organizations, were also described by integrative analyses of the ST data.

Our study reveals that the LN metastasis of NSCLC involves a complicated TME where cancer cell stemness, malignant-cell-derived-immunoglobulins, cancer associated fibroblast (CAF) cells, epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), immune evasion mechanisms as well as cellular and spatial interactions are involved. Additionally, it serves as a comprehensive data resource for understanding the mechanisms of metastatic and immune evasion involved in LN metastatic NSCLC.

## Results

The TME landscape of matched mLNs and mLN+ PTs in NSCLC
To characterize the TME characteristics involved in LN metastasis of NSCLC, we collected mLN (n= 22) and matched mLN+ PT samples (n=20) from 19 NSCLC patients (P0-P18) for scRNA-seq analysis, where matched mLN+ N samples (n=4) were also collected (Fig. 1A, created by BioGDP.com 34). In addition, to explore relevant spatial characteristics, we collected mLNs (n=4) and matched mLN+ PTs (n=4) from 4 of the 19 NSCLC patients for ST analysis (Fig. 1A, Methods). Meanwhile, public scRNA-seq datasets of mLN- samples including mLN- PT, mLN- N and nLN samples, and ST data of mLN- PT samples (De Zuani et al. 21, Zhang et al., 28, Kim et al. 23) were collected for integration and comparison (Fig. 1A). The clinicopathological information of the collected LN metastatic NSCLC patients was provided in Supplementary Data 1.

For the scRNA-seq data, 848337 single cells (334956 cells from the self-generated dataset, 513381 cells from the public datasets) passed quality controls in total. We confirmed the batch effects were corrected (Supplementary Fig. 1A, the bias of the nLN cells were due to the absence of epithelial cells in nLNs). As results, 9 major cell types were identified based on whether each cluster show specific expressions of canonical cell markers: B (CD79A, MS4A1), T (CD3D, CD3E, TRBC2), endothelial (CLDN5, PECAM1), epithelial (EPCAM, KRT17, KRT19), fibroblast (ACTA2, COL1A1, COL1A2), mast (TPSAB1, TPSB2), myeloid (LYZ, CD68, APOE), natural killer (NK) (NKG7, KLRB1, KLRD1), and plasma (MZB1, JCHAIN) 23, 27 (Fig. 1B and Supplementary Fig. 1B, 1C). Differences in cellular compositions across different samples, particularly between mLN+ PTs and mLN- PTs, as well as mLNs and nLNs, were observed. Notably, mLN+ PTs exhibited a higher prevalence of epithelial and plasma cells, while mLNs showed an increased proportion of B cells. In contrast, mLN- PTs had a greater abundance of myeloid cells, and nLNs had a higher proportion of T cells (Fig. 1C). These observations suggest that the TME undergoes alterations at both the primary and metastatic sites during LN metastasis.

For the ST data, there were 48535 spatial spots across the 4 pairs of mLNs (15401 spots) and mLN+ PTs (14082 spots) and the other 8 mLN- PTs (19052 spots). BayesSpace-based 35 spatial clustering analysis identified 21 different clusters (Supplementary Fig. 1D), and the clusters were annotated based on their marker genes (Fig. 1D, 1E and Supplementary Fig. 1D, 1E, Methods). For example, spatial cluster SC1 showed elevated expressions of SFTPC, SCIGB3A1, SCGB3A2, and SFTPB - all classical marker genes of lung epithelial cells - and was therefore annotated as epithelial-dominant (Supplementary Fig. 1D). For spatial clusters SC18 and SC19, which showed co-expressions of marker genes for both myeloid (LYZ, C1QB) and plasma cells (IGHG1, JCHAIN), the dominant cell types were defined as Myeloid+Plasma (Supplementary Fig. 1D), implying the co-localization of myeloid cells and plasma cells. Notably, two of the spatial clusters (SC3 and SC4) showed simultaneous high expressions of MS4A1, TRBC2 (Fig. 1D and Supplementary Fig. 1D), indicating the aggregation of T and B cells 36. The two clusters also showed high expressions of CXCL13, CCL19 and CCL21 (Supplementary Fig. 1D), all of which contribute to the formation of secondary and tertiary LS (TLS) 37, 38, 39. These two clusters were annotated as LS-like spots, representing the residual LSs in the mLNs, and potential TLSs in the mLN+ PTs or mLN- PTs. The spatial organizations of LS-like spots showed differences, with LS-like spots being more spatially aggregated in the mLN+ PTs than the mLN- PTs (Fig. 1F and Supplementary Fig. 1F). Additionally, epithelial cells typically exhibited spatial aggregation and with close proximity with fibroblasts, while sparse immune cell infiltrations into epithelial cells were observed, especially for the mLNs and mLN+ PTs (Fig. 1D, 1F).

Epithelial cells in mLNs and mLN+ PTs exhibit enhanced cancer stemness
We next re-clustering the epithelial cells and identified 7 types of epithelial cell sub-populations based on the canonical markers of lung epithelial cells 40: alveolar type I (AT1) (AGER, CLIC5), alveolar type II (AT2) (SFTPA1, SFTPA2, SFTPB, SCGB3A2), basal (KRT5, KRT15), ciliated (CAPS, TPPP3), club (SCGB1A1, SCGB3A1), and the other uncharacterized epithelial cells which were mainly patient specific (Fig. 2A and Supplementary Fig. 2A-2C, Methods). LUAD and LUSC were respectively dominant by AT2 and basal cells, as previously reported 28 (Fig. 2A, 2B). As expected, the epithelial cell compositions of mLNs were similar with those from the matched mLN+ PTs (Fig. 2B).

Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are important for tumor initiation, proliferation and metastasis 41. We evaluated cell stemness of the epithelial cells using CytoTRACE which can predict differentiation states of cells from scRNA-seq data, with higher scores representing higher stemness (Fig. 2C, 2D, Methods). Our findings revealed that epithelial cells in mLNs exhibited the highest CytoTRACE scores, and mLN+ PTs also demonstrated elevated CytoTRACE scores compared to other samples (Fig. 2C). This indicates a higher degree of stemness in the epithelial cells within both mLNs and mLN+ PTs.

CD44, EpCAM and CD166 (gene names CD44, EPCAM and ALCAM) are widely recognized markers of CSCs in NSCLC 42, 43. Here, epithelial cells exhibiting high CytoTRACE scores also showed a significant higher expressions of CD44, EPCAM and ALCAM (Fig. 2E). Additionally, a series of genes, such as FTH1, FTL, ENO1 and PKM, displayed strong correlations with the CytoTRACE based cell stemness (Fig. 2D, 2F). FTL and FTH1, which encode ferritin light chain and heavy chain respectively, are responsible in iron storage and involved in ferroptosis 44. Meanwhile, FTL and FTH1 along with multiple other ferroptosis relevant genes (PCBP1, PCBP2, SLC7A11, SLC3A2 and GPX4 45) were up-regulated in the epithelial cells of mLN and mLN+ PT samples compared to the mLN+ N samples (Supplementary Fig. 2D). The interplay between iron metabolism and CSC stemness or metastasis has been reported 46, 47. ENO1 has been demonstrated to improve the stemness of CSCs by promoting glycolysis in gastric cancer 48. Pyruvate kinase M2 isoform (PKM2) is capable of modulating the activity of key stemness regulators like c-Myc, and β-catenin, which are crucial for maintaining CSC phenotype 49, 50.

Furthermore, we utilized gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) to identify CSC relevant pathways (Methods). Our analysis revealed that the cell stemness in both LUAD and LUSC was significantly associated with MYC target signatures and a variety of metabolic pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), fatty acid metabolism, glycolysis and reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Fig. 2G). C-Myc has been reported to play an importance role in cell stemness 50, 51. CSCs exhibit high metabolic plasticity and can switch between OXPHOS and glycolysis in response to TME conditions 52, 53. ROS and fatty acid metabolism are also crucial for CSC survival and are linked to iron metabolism 46, 54, 55. We also established a CSC score for the bulk RNA-seq data based on the CSC relevant genes (Methods), and observed that a high CSC score was related with un-favorable overall survival in multiple cancer types (Fig. 2H and Supplementary Fig. 2E, 2F).

Elevated expression of immunoglobulin genes in epithelial cells of mLNs and mLN+ PTs
To further explore the specific properties of epithelial cells within the matched mLNs and mLN+ PTs, we compared the gene expressions of epithelial cells from the matched mLNs and mLN+ PTs to the other samples including mLN- PTs, mLN- Ns and mLN+ Ns. As expected, some of the CSC-relevant genes like FTL, HSPB1 and PABPC1 also showed higher expressions in the matched mLNs and mLN+ PTs than the other samples (Fig. 3A). Interestingly, we also observed elevated expression of multiple immunoglobulin relevant genes including IGHA1, IGHG1, IGHG4 and IGLC2, considering both AT2 and basal cells (Fig. 3A, 3B). The ST data also demonstrated that the elevated expression of immunoglobulin genes in the epithelial spots of the mLNs and mLN+ PTs when compared to mLN- PTs (Supplementary Fig. 3A). The immunoglobulin genes are typically expressed by B/plasma cells, which are known for their ability to produce and secrete antibodies. However, some studies have reported the presence of immunoglobulin expressions in tumor cells, challenging the notion that B/plasma cells are the sole source of immunoglobulins 56. To validate the elevated immunoglobulin gene expressions, we performed comparative analysis using the two public scRNA-seq datasets (De Zuani et al. [21], Zhang et al., [28], Methods). The results confirmed that the elevated expressions of immunoglobulin genes in the epithelial cells of mLN+ PTs than mLN- PTs (Supplementary Fig. 3B, 3C). These results underscore the potential involvement of immunoglobulins in LN metastatic of NSCLC.

Additionally, epithelial cells in the matched mLNs and mLN+ PTs were further divided into malignant and non-malignant based on copy number variations (CNVs) (Supplementary Fig. 3D, Methods). The CNV profiles also showed that malignant cells from one mLN were similar with the mLN+ PT from the same individual, while different patients exhibited divergences (Supplementary Fig. 3D). Malignant cells also showed higher expressions of immunoglobulin genes than the non-malignant epithelial cells (Fig. 3C). Meanwhile, we conducted parallel clustering analyses of malignant cells - one preserving patient-specific batch effects and one with batch effect correction, to ensure robust results (Methods). Both results showed that some of the clusters presented elevated expressions of immunoglobulin genes than the other clusters (Fig. 3D-3F and Supplementary Fig. 3E-3G). Notably, the malignant cells expressing high levels of immunoglobulin genes displayed significantly lower CytoTRACE scores than those with low immunoglobulin expressions (Fig. 3G and Supplementary Fig. 3H). This suggests that immunoglobulin genes are more likely to be expressed by cells with lower stemness, indicating the independent roles of CSCs and immunoglobulin-high malignant cells. Meanwhile, GSEA results showed these immunoglobulin-high malignant cells showed down-regulations of P53 pathway and apoptosis pathways (Fig. 3H), indicating its high proliferation ability. Various CSC-relevant metabolism pathways like fatty acid metabolism, ROS were down-regulated in the immunoglobulin-high malignant cells (Fig. 3H).

Importantly, these immunoglobulin-high malignant cells also exhibited significantly elevated expressions of CD274 (Fig. 3I and Supplementary Fig. 3I) which encodes the key immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1. The up-regulations of PD-L1 can facilitate T cell suppression. In addition, an integrative analysis incorporating scRNA-seq data of metastasis brain (mBrain) from LUAD manifested that the immunoglobulin genes were also highly expressed by mBrain sites (Fig. 3J and Supplementary Fig. 3J, Methods), indicating the potential role of malignant-cell-derived-immunoglobulins in secondary dissemination to distant organs.

We also investigated spatially dependent characteristics of epithelial cells in the mLNs and mLN+ PTs. The epithelial spots were further categorized into core and peripheral tumor regions based on their proximity to non-epithelial spots (Fig. 3K and Supplementary Fig. 3K, Methods). Notably, the peripheral region showed significant up-regulations of immunoglobulin genes, collagen genes (COL1A1, COL1A2) and major histocompatibility class I subunit genes (B2M and HLA-A) (Fig. 3L, 3M). In contrast, the tumor core regions had higher CytoTRACE scores compared to the peripheral regions (Supplementary Fig. 3L). Pathway enrichment analysis revealed that the up-regulated genes in the peripheral regions were enriched by EMT, and immune relevant pathways like interferon gamma response, while the core regions were enriched by CSC-relevant pathways like MYC targets, fatty acid metabolism and OXPHOS (Fig. 3N). NicheNet analyses identified several ligands including TGFB1, TGFB2 and BMP4 which were likely driving the target gene expressions of the EMT-dominated tumor peripheral regions (Fig. 3O).

Fibroblasts form a cell transition niche and immune barrier in the leading edge of tumors in mLNs and mLN+ PTs
Stromal cells were categorized into sub-populations based on specific marker genes of fibroblasts 57 and endothelial cells (ECs) 58, including matrix CAF (mCAF) (MMP11, COL1A1), inflammatory CAF (iCAF) (CFD, C3), vascular CAF (vCAF) (COL18A1, NOTCH3), tumor-like CAF (tCAF) (GAPDH, ENO1), smooth muscle cell (SMC) (TAGLN, ACTA2), pericyte (RGS5, NOTCH3), aerocytes (HPGD), arterial EC (HEY1, IGFBP3), capilary EC (CA4), EC progenitor (CD34, KDR), lymphatic (LYVE1, CCL21), venous (ACKR1) and proliferation stromal (MKI67). Additionally, CST1+ fibroblasts showed specific high expressions of CST1, WIF1, COL8A1 and COL10A1 (Fig. 4A and Supplementary Fig. 4A, 4B, Methods). CST1 (Cystatin 1) is a protease inhibitor. CST1 overexpression has been observed in various cancer types 59, 60, 61. Its role in inhibiting cysteine proteases suggests a potential function in modulating the extracellular matrix. The CST1+ fibroblasts have also been identified in tumor tissues of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, and show prognostic values 61. Here, the CST1+ fibroblasts were specific to mLNs and mLN+ PTs in LUAD. Moreover, the mCAFs predominated in primary tumors, iCAFs were more enriched by normal lung tissues, vCAFs were most abundant in the mLNs (Fig. 4B). Endothelial cell populations in the mLNs closely resembled those in the mLN+ PTs, with venous ECs being dominant, whereas LECs were most common in the nLNs (Fig. 4C). Additionally, cell-cell communication analysis revealed that the mCAFs/vCAFs interacted with the malignant cells through various collages in both mLNs (Fig. 4D) and mLN+ PTs (Supplementary Fig. 4C). The main receptors of the malignant cells included SDC1, SDC4, CD44 and integrin genes. Previous studies have reported that SDC1 plays as role in the activation of CSCs 62. Meanwhile, the collagen-integrin interactions can help malignant cells to invade blood vessels and develop a metastatic niche in distant organs 63. Among the fibroblast sub-populations, the mCAFs and CST1+ fibroblasts had higher cell transition scores than the others (Fig. 4E, Methods).

Notably, the mLNs or mLN+ PTs exhibited elevated expressions of the vCAF marker genes (COL8A1, COL18A1 and IGFBP7) and several cell transition relevant genes like TGFBI, AMBRA1 and PLEKHA7 compared to the other sample types in the stromal cells (Fig. 4F and Supplementary Fig. 4D). AMBRA1 plays a key role in tumorigenesis and progression through regulating the autophagy process, cell transition and a variety of processes 64. PLEKHA7 regulates the assembly of cytoplasmic apical zonula adherens junctions, thereby maintaining cell-cell adhesion and tight-junction 65. TGFBI was up-regulated in the mLN+ PTs than the mLN- PTs (Fig. 4F). TGF-β as a cytokine can secret and is critical for epithelia cell transition. Meanwhile, its role in the exclusion of CD8+ T cells from tumor core areas has been demonstrated 66. ST-based analysis revealed that fibroblast spots were with significantly higher CCNs with epithelial spots (p=0.00012, W = 249, 95 % confident interval = [-366, -135], by unpaired two-sided Wilcoxon test) than other spots, suggesting that fibroblasts are with closer proximity to the epithelial cells than the other cells, particularly in the mLN+ PTs (Fig. 4G). Immune cells were relatively far from the tumor cores, being separated by the fibroblasts, rather than infiltrated into the tumor cells in mLNs and mLN+ PTs (Fig. 1D). Meanwhile, the proportions of fibroblasts, especially mCAF and tCAF cells showed negative correlations with both T and B cells (Fig. 4H). These findings suggest the fibroblasts may form an immune exclusion barrier in the leading edge of tumor cells during LN metastasis in NSCLC.

Considering the specificity of the CST1+ fibroblasts in the mLNs and mLN+ PTs, we examined the spatial expressions of CST1 in different samples. The mLNs and mLN+ PTs also exhibited elevated expression of CST1 compared to the mLN- PTs based on the ST data (Fig. 4I, 4J and Supplementary Fig. 4E). Pathway enrichment analysis revealed that expression of CST1 was significantly associated with cell transition process (Supplementary Fig. 4FL). Additionally, several other cell transition-relevant genes like CTGF 67, ISLR 68 and SMOC2 69 also showed elevated expressions in the mLN+ PTs based on the ST data (Fig. 4I). These up-regulated genes were significantly enriched by pathways like EMT and interferon response pathways (Fig. 4K). NicheNet analysis identified the potential ligands for CST1 and the other up-regulated genes of mLN+ PTs included JAG1, INHBA, IL25 and IL4 (Fig. 4L). Meanwhile, fibroblasts in close proximity to epithelial cells showed significantly higher CST1 expressions than those located far away (Fig. 4M). These findings suggest the role of fibroblasts, especially the CST1+ fibroblasts, in promoting cell transition in LN metastatic NSCLC.

Role of myeloid cells in immune suppression and LS formation in mLNs and mLN+ PTs
Re-clustering analysis of the myeloid cells identified 11 sub-populations based on the marker genes of macrophage (MP), dendritic cell (DC), monocyte 70 and some specific genes including SPP1, FABP4, GPNMB and LAMP3 (Fig. 5A-5C and Supplementary Fig. 5A, Methods). Both SPP1 71 and GPNMB 72 have been reported to facilitate the polarization of M2 macrophages which supports tumor progression by producing immunosuppressive cytokines in MPs, while FABP4 is mainly produced by alveolar macrophages which play a key role in innate immune response against infection 73. Here, FABP4+ MPs were abundant in normal lungs, while SPP1+ MPs were more enriched by primary tumors and mLNs, and GPNMB+ MPs were more enriched by the mLNs and mLN+ PTs of LUAD (Fig. 5C, 5D). Further comparing mLNs to nLNs and mLN+ PTs to mLN- PTs, it was observed that both mLNs and mLN+ PTs exhibited larger proportions of SPP1+ MP and neutrophil (Neu) cells compared to their respective controls (Fig. 5D). Meanwhile, the high expression of SPP1 was associated with unfavorable prognosis in LUAD (Fig. 5E, Methods). Notably, the proportion of SPP1+ MP cells, rather than the other sub-populations of MP cells, showed a strong correlation with the proportion of malignant cells (Fig. 5F).

Further comparisons of the gene expressions of the SPP1+ MPs across different sample types discovered that certain genes including IFI30, FOS, HSPA1A, IGHG4, CCL3, CCL4, etc., were specifically up-regulated in the mLNs and mLN+ PTs (Fig. 5G). Meanwhile, clustering analysis of the SPP1+ MPs identified a cluster predominantly enriched by mLNs and mLN+ PTs, with a particular prevalence in the mLNs (Supplementary Fig. 5B-D). This cluster also showed significantly up-regulated expressions of IFI30 along with the other aforementioned genes (Supplementary Fig. 5D). IFI30, also known as gamma interferon-inducible lysosomal thiolredoxin, is mainly expressed in antigen-presenting cells, including MP, DC and B cells 74. Recent studies have revealed that IFI30 can promote tumor metastasis and immune evasion in cancer 75, 76. Remarkably, overexpression of IFI30 has been shown to promote the M2 polarization of MPs and increase the expression of PD-L1 in breast cancer 75. In our findings, we also observed that CD274 was up-regulated in the SPP1+ IFI30+ MPs (Supplementary Fig. 5E). Additionally, the SPP1+IFI30+ MPs also showed up-regulated expressions of GABARAP, MIF, TNFRSF13, etc. (Fig. 5H). These genes have been demonstrated to promote the M2 polarization of MPs 77, 78, 79. Among them, MIF is a pro-inflammatory cytokine that plays a crucial role in various immune processes 78, and TNFSF13 (also known as APRIL), a proliferation-inducing ligand of the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) superfamily, has emerged as a promising target for countering immunosuppression 79. Moreover, cell-cell communication analysis revealed that the SPP1+ MPs interacted with the malignant cells through MIF (Supplementary Fig. 5F, 5G) and interacted with the T cells, through CXCL9-CXCR3 and CXCL16-CXCR6 axes (Fig. 5I). Spatial examination of cellular distributions indicated a non-co-localization pattern between SPP1+ MP and malignant cells, suggesting potential long-range interactions mediated by paracrine or endocrine signaling 80 (Supplementary Fig. 5H, 5I). In contrast, SPP1+ MP and T cell sub-populations exhibited co-localization, indicating short-range cellular crosstalk (Supplementary Fig. 5H, 5I).

Based on the ST data, the myeloid-relevant spots (myeloid/plasma+myeloid spots) were categorized into far and near groups, based on their distance from epithelial cells (see Methods). The analysis showed that myeloid spots in close proximity to epithelial cells exhibited higher expression levels of CXCL9, PGK1 and SPP1, while those farther away showed higher expressions of IFI30, APOE and GPNMB (Fig. 5J), indicating the spatial distinct characteristics of myeloid cells. Moreover, the myeloid cell spots were divided into 7 spatial clusters (SCs) (Methods), and the spatial cluster 7 (SC7), which was in close proximity to LS-like spots, showed remarkably high expression of CCL21 and CCL18 (Fig. 5K, 5L and Supplementary Fig. 6A). Meanwhile, the SC7 was more enriched by the mLNs (Supplementary Fig. 6B). Most of the marker genes were primarily expressed by the GPNMB+ MPs or SPP1+ MPs, while CCL21 and CPVL were also highly- expressed by DCs (Supplementary Fig. 6C). The chemokines CCL21 and CCL18 play important roles in immune cell trafficking and are both involved in the formation and function of TLSs 81. CCL18 can also contribute to immune suppression when it attracts T regulatory (Treg) cells 82 and M2-like MPs 83.

Reduction of anti-tumor immunity through T cell exhaustion and immune exclusion
T and NK cells were further classified into 12 sub-populations (Fig. 6A, Methods). In addition to some well-defined sub-populations including CD4 effector memory T, CD4 naïve T, CD4 resident effector memory T, Treg, CD8 cytotoxic T, CD8 exhausted T as well as NK cells, we also identified several other sub-populations (Fig. 6A and Supplementary Fig. 7A, Methods). Sub-populations showing specific high expressions of ALDOA, ARHGAP15 and CXCL13 were defined by the gene names (Fig 6A and Supplementary Fig. 7A, 7B). A small sub-population which also showed specific high expressions of HAVCR2, TIGIT, CTLA4, classical markers of T cell exhaustion, but with differential expression profiles from the CD8 exhausted T cells, was defined as “other exhausted T cells” (Supplementary Fig. 7A). This sub-population was specific in the mLNs (Supplementary Fig. 7C). Some CXCL13+ T cells are characterized as follicular helper (Tfh) 84 or exhausted T cells 85 by recent studies. Here, the CXCL13+ T cells showed specific high expressions of CXCL13, ICA1, IL6ST, CTLA4 and PDCD1, however, BCL6 and CXCR5, two classical marker genes of Tfh cells 86, were not highly expressed (Supplementary Fig. 7A, 7B). The CXCL13+ T cells also exhibited the highest exhaustion scores among the T cells (Fig. 6C, Methods), and showed high expressions of exhaustion marker genes like CTLA4 87 and PDCD1 88 (Fig. 6D and Supplementary Fig. 7B), highlighting its exhausted state. Both mLNs and mLN+ PTs contained more Tregs and CXCL13+ T cells than other sample types (Fig. 6B and Supplementary Fig. 7C). ALDOA, or Aldolase A, is an enzyme crucial for glycolysis and gluconeogenesis which are important for maintaining cellular energy balance, and ALDOA expression may influence T cell behavior 89, potentially affecting their ability to effectively target and eliminate cancer cells 90. The ALDOA+ T cells were predominantly enriched by nLNs, but significantly reduced in mLNs (Fig. 6B), strongly suggests a state of metabolic impairment or dysfunction, contributing to the ineffective anti-tumor response in mLNs. ARHGAP15, a gene encoding a Rho GTPase-activating protein, can inhibit Rac1 activity 91. Rac1 is a small GTPase involved in various cellular processes, including T cell activation and migration 92. ARHGAP15+ T cells were more enriched in mLNs and mLN+ PTs (Fig. 6B), indicating suppression of T cell activation and motility, offering a plausible mechanism for their trapped and dysfunctional state. The mLNs were mainly composed of CD4 T cells, especially CD4 naïve T cells, while the mLN+ PTs contained more CD8 exhausted T cells (Fig. 6B and Supplementary Fig. 7C). Moreover, the LS-like spots exhibited higher expressions of the CXCL13+ T relevant genes including CTLA4, CXCL13, PDCD1 and TRBC2 than other spatial spots (Fig. 6E). The CXCL13+ T cells were primarily enriched by the LS-like spots based on the deconvolution analysis of ST data (Fig. 6F and Supplementary Fig. 7D). Notably, the LS-like spots in the mLNs and mLN+ PTs showed significantly higher exhaustion scores than the mLN- PTs (Fig. 6G). Taken together, the anti-tumor cytotoxicity of T cells in both mLNs and mLN+ PTs appears to be reduced by Tregs and exhausted T cells.

CXCL13 is strongly associated with the aggregation of T and B cells, and it plays a pivotal role in the formation of secondary LSs in LNs and TLSs in tumors 93. The gene ontology (GO) based pathway enrichment analysis revealed the CXCL13+ T cells were associated with B cell receptor signaling pathway, indicting its ability to recruit B cells. Cell-cell communication analysis revealed that the CXCL13+ T cells can interact with the B cells via the CXCL13-CXCR5 axis (Fig. 6H), while the CAF and LAMP3+ DC cells can interact with the CXCL13+ T cells through the CCL19-CCR7 axis (Fig. 6I). CARD-based deconvolution analysis of the ST data also showed CXCL13+ T cells were significantly co-localized with key interacting cells, including LAMP3+ DCs, GC B cells, and activated B cells, within LS-like spots (Supplementary Fig. 7E, 7F). While spatial distributions of iCAF and mCAF cells were broader (Supplementary Fig. 7E), and did not show significant enrichment in LS-like spots (Supplementary Fig. 7F), suggesting that their interaction with CXCL13+ T cells might be less constrained to the core LS-like architecture. Additionally, we also found the CXCL13+ T cells and Tregs were more enriched by the mLN+ PTs from NSCLC patients without smoking history comparing to those with smoking history (Supplementary Fig. 7G).

The B and plasma cells were further characterized into sub-populations based on the re-clustering analysis (Fig. 6J and Supplementary Fig. 8A, Methods). The mLNs contained more activated B cells, while the mLN+ Ns and mLN+ PTs contained a large fraction of plasma cells (Fig. 6K), indicating the activation of B cell mediated adaptive immune responses during LN metastasis in NSCLC. The plasma cells in the mLN+ PTs showed frequent interactions with malignant cells and mCAFs (Fig. 6L). However, the excess activated B cells and plasma cells in mLNs and mLN+ PTs indicated prolonged activation of B cells which can lead to immune dysfunction or exhausted B cell states 94. Plasma cells can produce antibodies to recognize and attack tumor cells. Further clustering analysis of the plasma cells revealed that the mLN+ PTs and mLN- PTs were respectively enriched by the Plasma_C2 and Plasma_C1 clusters (Fig 6M, 6N). The two clusters showed distinct immunoglobin expression patterns, with Plasma_C2 showing significantly higher expressions of IGHG4 and IGHV4-34, whereas Plasma_C1 showing higher expressions of IGHA2, IGHG2 and IGKC (Fig. 6O and Supplementary Fig. 8B), indicating remarkable differences between the antibody isotypes of plasma cells from mLN+ PTs and mLN- PTs. Moreover, since the malignant cells in the mLNs and mLN+ PTs also exhibited high expressions of IGHG4 (Fig. 3B), it is possible that the malignant-cell-derived IgG neutralizes the plasma-cell-derived IgG to inhibit complement-dependent cytotoxicity, thereby preventing host immune system and promoting tumor growth, as revealed previously 95. Deconvolution analysis of B cell sub-populations revealed that the LS-like spots were enriched with germinal center (GC) B cells, a hallmark of mature TLS 96, while few plasma cells in the LS-like spots (Supplementary Fig. 8C). The proportions of GC B cells in the mLNs were significantly higher than the mLN+ PTs (Supplementary Fig. 8D), indicating the TLSs in the mLN+ PTs may be immature.

To further characterize the TME surrounding the LS-like spots, we extracted the two-step neighbors of each LS-like spot (Fig. 6P, Methods). In the mLNs and mLN+ PTs, the neighbors of the LS-like spots were primarily other LS-like spots (Fig. 6P, 6Q), indicating the spatial aggregation of the LS-like spots. Meanwhile, the LS-like regions in the mLN- PTs were more likely to be infiltrated into epithelial cells (Fig. 6P), however, fewer LS-like regions were infiltrated into the tumor areas in the mLNs and the mLN+ PTs, with fibroblast or myeloid cells forming an immune-excluded 97 interface between the tumor and immune cells (Fig. 1E, 4G, 6P). These findings together described a complex immunosuppressive TME that caused by the immune exhaustion states and spatial organizations.

Distinct cellular mechanisms involved in lymph node metastasis between LUAD and LUSC
To further investigate the differences between LUAD and LUSC regarding LN metastasis, we quantified cell composition changes of mLN+ PT comparing to either normal lung or mLN- PT tissues in LUAD and LUSC samples respectively. Both conserved and specific cellular features were identified (Supplementary Fig. 9). Notably, mLN+ PTs of LUAD displayed significant accumulation of ARHGAP15+ T, CXCL13+ T, plasma and Treg cells. In contrast, mLN+ PTs of LUSC displayed depletion of various effector immune cells, particularly CD4 effector T cells and NK cells (Supplementary Fig. 9). CAFs, such as vCAF and tCAF, were consistently enriched by the mLN+ PT samples in both LUAD and LUSC, suggesting a similar stromal response. These divergent immune landscapes suggest fundamentally distinct metastatic mechanisms - where LUAD is more likely to develop an immunosuppressive niche through Treg and exhausted lymphocytes, while LUSC appears to evade immunity more by immune cell exclusion.

Validations of key TME characteristics associated with LN metastasis in NSCLC
First, we examined the CSC relevant gene signatures in multiple independent scRNA-seq datasets of NSCLC. In the GSE127465 dataset 98, the epithelial cells from the primary tumors at the N1 stage exhibited significantly higher CSC scores and up-regulated expressions of the CSC relevant genes compared to those at the N0 stage (Fig. 7A). Meanwhile, analysis of datasets GSE123904 99 and GSE131907 23 demonstrated that epithelial cells derived from distant metastatic sites and mLNs consistently showed higher CSC scores and increased expression of CSC-associated genes than both primary tumor cells and normal lung tissues (Fig. 7B, 7C and Supplementary Fig. 10A). These results indicate the CSCs play important roles in both LN and distant metastasis.

Furthermore, to investigate the general expressional patterns and prognostic effects of the various signature genes identified in this study, we performed clustering analysis of the TCGA-LUAD tumor samples based on the bulk RNA-seq data of the signature genes (Methods). Four bulk RNA-seq data based clusters (BCs) were identified, where the cluster BC3 showed the most un-favorable prognosis (Fig. 7D, 7E and Supplementary Fig. 10B). Genes up-regulated in BC3 included several CSC relevant genes like FTH1, GPX2, AKR1C1, AKR1C2 and AKR1C3. Up-regulation of these genes like GPX2, AKR1C1 have been demonstrated to inhibit ferroptosis 100, 101. FTH1, a key regulator in iron storage, was identified as one top-ranked CSC-relevant gene in both LUAD and LUSC (Fig. 2D, 2E). Moreover, mBrain and mLN samples showed higher expressions of FTH1 than normal lung tissues, and primary tumors in the epithelial cells (Fig. 7F). The prognostic significance of BC3 was validated by the other two independent bulk RNA-seq datasets, which respectively included NSCLC and LUAD tumor samples (Supplementary Fig. 10C, 10D). Meanwhile, the BC3 displayed a higher prevalence of metastatic LNs than the other BCs in the two datasets (Supplementary Fig. 10E).

To validate FTH1 and immunoglobulin gene relevant functions both in vitro and in vivo, we conducted loss-of function analyses of FTH1 and IGHG4 in lung cancer cell lines (Fig. 7G and Supplementary Fig. 10F). Notably, FTH1 and IGHG4 knockdown reduced the several EMT marker genes expression of Vimentin, N-cadherin, MMP2/9, ZEB1/2 and Twist in A549 and H460 cells, while increasing E-cadherin expression increased in FTH1 knockdown cells (Fig. 7G and Supplementary Fig. 10F). Furthermore, two independent FTH1 short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) significantly decreased the proliferation of A549 and H460 cells (Supplementary Fig. 10G). However, IGHG4 knockdown did not influenced A549 and H460 cell proliferation (Supplementary Fig. 10H). Interestingly, treatment with the ferroptosis inducer Erastin did not further enhance ferroptosis-dependent growth inhibition in FTH1 knock-downed lung cancer cells (Supplementary Fig.10I, 10J). Additionally, FTH1 and IGHG4 knockdown decreased cell invasion in both A549 and H460 cells (Fig. 7H and Supplementary Fig. 10K, 10L). In vivo, FTH1 knockdown cells formed fewer metastatic lung nodules compared to control cells, with no significant changes in body weight observed during the metastatic colonization assay (Fig. 7I, 7J and Supplementary Fig. 10M). Collectively, these findings prove that FTH1 and IGHG4 play crucial regulatory roles in lung cancer metastasis.

We further analyzed the expression profiles of SPP1+IFI30+ MP and CXCL13+ T cells across the validation datasets. Notably, the primary tumors at the N1 stage demonstrated significantly higher scores considering the SPP1+IFI30+ MP and CXCL13+ T relevant gene signatures in the myeloid and T cells compared to those at the N0 stage (Fig. 7K). This pattern was consistently observed in distant metastatic lesions and mLN samples, which exhibited higher scores for both immune cell types (Fig. 7L, 7M). The expressional signatures of these two immune cell types, especially the SPP1+IFI30+ MP, showed strong positive correlations with the CSC signature (Supplementary Fig. 10N). Supporting these findings, both parental and sixth-generation LN samples derived from LN metastasis mouse models 14 maintained elevated expression scores for these immune cell populations (Supplementary Fig. 10O). These results highlight the potential significance of SPP1+IFI30+ MP and CXCL13+ T cells in facilitating NSCLC metastasis. Moreover, analysis of an independent NSCLC cohort 102 revealed that elevated signature scores of SPP1+ IFI30+ macrophages and CXCL13+ T cells in pre-treatment non-responders to immuno-chemotherapy (Supplementary Fig. 11A, 11B), suggesting their associations with resistance to immuno-chemotherapy.

We further examined our findings in the mLNs of breast cancer based on ST data 32. Similar to NSCLC, mLNs of breast cancer also exhibited residual LSs (LS-like spots defined based on high expressions of CXCL13, CCL19, CCL21 and MS4A1, Supplementary Fig. 12A-12F), with significantly elevated CXCL13+ T cell signature scores (Supplementary Fig. 12G). In addition, the mLNs of breast cancer also displayed significant higher expressions of SPP1 and IFI30, along with elevated SPP1+IFI30+ MP signature scores compared to nLNs (Supplementary Fig. 13A-13E). These conserved features suggest a potential universal role for SPP1+IFI30+ MP and CXCL13+ T cells in LN metastasis across multiple cancer types.
